episodes.213037: Scattered thunderstorms developed across Middle Tennessee on June 22, 2026. Heavy rain was reported in Lawrenceburg which caused minor flooding with one road closure.
episodes.213084: Heavy rain produced localized flooding across northwest Indiana from the afternoon of June 21st into the early morning of June 22nd.
episodes.213096: The 21st late day brought a quickly-evolving set-up featuring an increasingly moist column supported by an approaching Middle Mississippi Valley upper short wave trough, strengthening flow amid a warm frontal zone draped over the local central Indiana region providing 35-50KT of effective wind shear, and advection of higher low-level dewpoints with daytime heating which provided sufficient destabilization.  Severe rotating supercells tracked across Illinois into southern central Indiana as they aligned into a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).||Wind damage occurred within nine central Indiana zones and as far east as Brown County, five (mainly EF-0) tornadoes were focused in Owen County and points south and west, while the region's farthest southwestern counties experienced scattered flash flooding following downpours from multiple supercells.  A final EF-0 torando and flash flooding also occurred in Bartholomew County.  This Bartholomew County EF-0 was Indiana's 63rd tornado in 2026...a new yearly state tornado record (73 events) was set later in the evening, with 74 tallied by the end of June 21st.
episodes.213186: A round of severe thunderstorms, a tornado and flash flooding occurred during the evening of June 21, lasting into the morning of June 22.
episodes.213274: Driven by a weak frontal zone over southern Oklahoma, two separate thunderstorm complexes tracked from west to east over the same areas, causing flash flooding across Lamar County. The bulk of the flooding occurred on June 23 in connection with the second complex. The systems also produced isolated large hail and a single severe wind gust.
episodes.213298: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley on the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. A cold front was then dragged across the Middle Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians as the parent system continued onward towards the Mid-Atlantic Coast from the 22nd into the morning of the 23rd.||A band of precipitation moved into northeast Kentucky on the night of the 21st and then continued east into West Virginia early on the morning of the 22nd. Additional rounds of showers and a few strong thunderstorms continued to progress across the area during the day, then precipitation came to an end following the frontal passage overnight. Precipitation amounts across the area ranged from a few tenths up to an inch and a half with the highest amounts occurring in Lawrence, southern Carter, and southern Boyd counties.
episodes.213299: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley on the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. Isolated to scattered showers and a few strong thunderstorms continued to progress across the area during the day, then precipitation tapered off following the frontal passage late in the day. Showers and storms generally produced pockets of one to one and a half inches of rain accumulation, however training storms did lead to a strip of two to three inches in eastern Washington County.
episodes.213300: A low pressure system lifted a warm front through the area as it travelled out of the Central Plains and into the Ohio Valley the night of June 21st into the morning of the 22nd. Minor flooding also occurred on Island Creek near Logan.

episodes.213349: Lines of thunderstorms developing well out ahead of a cold front in a hot and unstable environment resulted in scattered instances of damaging wind gusts. A few destructive wind gusts were noted in north-central Virginia.
episodes.213355: Lines of thunderstorms developing well out ahead of a cold front in a hot and unstable environment resulted in scattered instances of gale-force wind gusts.
episodes.213458: Intense thunderstorms rapidly developed over Harper County during the late nighttime hours of June 21. These storms had up to quarter size hail and estimated wind gusts up to 100 mph. Structural damage included a stationary train derailment and significant damage to a small shop building.
episodes.213677: Although most of the activity was in western Nebraska, far eastern Wyoming experienced isolated severe thunderstorms with large hail and a few strong wind gusts reported. Severe thunderstorm Watch was in effect along and east of the Interstate 25 corridor for the afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.213763: A cold front moved through the combined Panhandles from north to south on the evening of June 21st. There was enough wind shear, instability and daytime heating to allow for thunderstorms to develop. Some of these storms were severe with damaging winds being the primary hazard.
episodes.213895: A cold frontal passage brought a line of showers and isolated thunderstorms to mainly southern Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours of June 22, 2026. Despite a favorable lifting mechanism, thunderstorms largely failed to organize into a cohesive line due to lack of favorable bulk shear and instability across the region. There was a narrow corridor of instability that exceeded 1000 J/kg across far western Pennsylvania that allowed for some storms to become marginally severe and produce damaging wind gusts as they came into Somerset County. Due to these thunderstorms, there were multiple reports of widespread trees and wires down near Confluence and Friedens before storms became weaker further east.
episodes.213986: Thunderstorms developed over western Kansas during the afternoon of the 21st, near a surface low pressure system and a quasi-stationary front. These thunderstorms organized into a line as they moved southeast across southern Kansas and northwest Oklahoma during the evening. Numerous damaging wind reports occurred across eastern Oklahoma during the early morning hours of the 22nd, as this squall line raced through the area.
episodes.213987: Thunderstorms developed over western Kansas during the afternoon of the 21st, near a surface low pressure system and a quasi-stationary front. These thunderstorms organized into a line as they moved southeast across southern Kansas and northwest Oklahoma during the evening. Several damaging wind reports and a tornado occurred across west central Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 22nd, as this squall line raced through the area.
episodes.214054: Atlantic high pressure ridge axis remained over the eastern Gulf, central FL and into the western Atlantic maintaining a moist west-southwest low level flow for the area. Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed each afternoon along the sea breezes with the strongest activity along boundary mergers. A weak cool front gradually moved southward through the area on Tuesday with a weak prefrontal trough from southwest to northeast over the region. Deeper moisture plume coincided with the frontal boundary with the strongest storms along the sea breeze and frontal interactions.
episodes.214148: An outflow-reinforced front moved into the area during the morning of June 22nd, and a dryline set up over west Texas. These features, combined with lift from a disturbance in the upper-level flow, yield thunderstorm development during the afternoon. One storm in rural Pecos County interacted with remnant surface vorticity from the decaying boundary and managed to produce a weak tornado. Another storm moved through Midland and produced up to ping-pong ball sized hail.
episodes.214306: An approaching warm front produced showers and thunderstorms over portions of the Delaware Valley up through northern New Jersey. A few of these storms produced heavy rain.
episodes.214307: An approaching warm front produced showers and thunderstorms over portions of the Delaware Valley up through northern New Jersey. A few of these storms produced heavy rain.
episodes.214352: An intense mesoscale convective system (MCS), later classified as a derecho, swept across much of Oklahoma and portions of western-north Texas during the late evening of the 21st and predawn hours of the 22nd. Widespread reports of thunderstorm wind damage were received, especially from northwestern into central Oklahoma, including several observations of 80-100 mph gusts. This system also produced several tornadoes in central Oklahoma, including an EF-2 tornado near El Reno, OK. A slow-moving supercell preceded the convective line during the mid-evening of the 21st, producing reports of large hail west of Woodward, OK before dissipating.
episodes.214477: Scattered thunderstorms tracked across northeast Colorado, producing hail as large as 2.75 inches in diameter.
episodes.214478: A supercell thunderstorm dropped south-southeast out of western Nebraska and continued to travel south-southeast across Logan and Washington Counties. As this storm moved through the Akron. Extreme winds in excess of 100 mph were reported just west of Akron, including a 109 mph wind gust at the Akron airport (AKO). Wind damage to trees and homes was observed.
episodes.214613: A cold front brought severe weather, heavy rain, and flash flooding to southeast Alabama.
episodes.214656: A slow moving frontal boundary affected the area during the June 18-22 period with multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms. Some severe weather was reported along with flash flooding.
episodes.214680: A stationary front draped across Arkansas in tandem with an approaching upper level trough axis would spur multiple days of severe winds, flash flooding, and heavy rain totals for the multi-day event across the state of Arkansas.
episodes.214940: A remnant Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV) interacted with a sheared and unstable environment to produce numerous supercells in southeast Illinois on June 21st.  13 tornadoes were documented, the strongest being two EF-2 tornadoes near Newton.  Storms training over the same areas led to widespread heavy rainfall and several occurrences of flash flooding.
episodes.214991: A Mesoscale Convective Complex (MCS) quickly shifted southeast across Central and Southeast Oklahoma during the early morning hours of June 22nd, driven by a strong southwesterly low level jet and an upper level disturbance that traversed the state. These storms began to weaken as they moved into Southeast Oklahoma, but remained strong enough to produce strong and locally damaging winds which downed several trees across McCurtain County Oklahoma shortly before daybreak.
episodes.215013: Supercell thunderstorms developed within the Black Hills and produced severe hail across much of Pennington County including at the NWS office.
episodes.215014: Thunderstorms developed around midday over the central Nebraska Panhandle. This activity tracked to the east and southeast into the evening hours, producing numerous damaging wind and large hail reports. The greatest damage was at the eastern end of Lake McConaughy. Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 81 MPH were reported. Hail up to golf ball size was reported near Imperial.
episodes.215030: Supercell thunderstorms impacted eastern Wyoming. The hardest hit was Campbell county where a supercell thunderstorm produced a damaging EF2 tornado.
episodes.215078: A slow moving cold front pushed into the Mid-South during the morning of June 22, 2026. A weak surface low pressure system tracked along the front and across the Mid-South as the front slowly moved across the area. Meanwhile, an upper level disturbance moving through the Lower Mississippi Valley helped to trigger widespread showers and thunderstorms along the front. Anomalously high precipitable water values of over 2 inches were pooled along the front resulting in heavy rainfall with some places reporting over 6 inches. Several areas experienced flash flooding.
episodes.215079: A slow moving cold front pushed into the Mid-South during the morning of June 22, 2026. A weak surface low pressure system tracked along the front and across the Mid-South as the front slowly moved across the area. Meanwhile, an upper level disturbance moving through the Lower Mississippi Valley helped to trigger widespread showers and thunderstorms along the front. Anomalously high precipitable water values of over 2 inches were pooled along the front resulting in heavy rainfall with some places reporting over 6 inches. Several areas experienced flash flooding.
episodes.215152: Two rounds of strong to severe thunderstorms took place during the afternoon and evening hours on the 22nd. A remnant mesoscale convective vortex, or MCV, crossed across Arkansas, Tennessee, and portions of Alabama and Georgia. Ahead of the MCV, strengthening winds aloft helped fuel thunderstorms. First round was of storms produced only isolated wind damage. Second round presented a strongly bowed cluster of storms which produced significant wind damage in portions of southeastern Tennessee, primarily in Hamilton County. Damages were north of at least $2 million.
episodes.215235: A line of severe storms moved across the state of Mississippi during the morning and afternoon hours of June 22 2026. Some of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts that downed trees and powerlines.
episodes.215295: A cold front draped over the Ohio Valley tracked into the central and southern Appalachians by the late evening and overnight period. Ahead of the front, scattered showers and storms tracked from the North Carolina mountains into the Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain during the evening hours. Numerous wind damage reports were observed over the Piedmont of central North Carolina.
episodes.215511: During the early evening hours on the 21st, a few clusters of thunderstorms moved southeast across portions of northwest Kansas. Hail up to one inch in diameter occurred in Thomas County, and wind gusts up to 70 mph occurred in Wichita County, downing numerous power poles.  A short lived tornado occurred in far northwest Thomas County on the leading edge of one of the storms.
episodes.215553: A narrow warm sector along and south of a nearly stationary boundary saw showers and thunderstorms develop in the afternoon hours. Training along the boundary mostly resulted in a flash flooding threat, though moisture pooling ahead of the front supported MLCAPE values reaching 1000 J/kg, and 30-40 knots of effective shear supported some storm organization for a damaging wind and embedded tornado threat with locally backed surface wind.
episodes.215556: A narrow warm sector along and south of a nearly stationary boundary saw showers and thunderstorms develop in the afternoon hours. episodes.215648: On the night of June 21st, 2026 and into the early morning of June 22nd, 2026, a Mesoscale Convective System moved through southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. This system brought multiple lines of storms and some supercells. Several tornadoes occurred along with flash flooding.
episodes.215660: A warm front approached from the south as multiple shortwaves moved through aloft. A few storms were able to become severe as a decent veering wind profile with sufficient speed shear was available. These storms produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.215697: Scattered to widespread storms developed across central Virginia in the afternoon of June 22. This was in associated with a lee trough and cold front well west of the region. Upscale growth into a few storm clusters produced swaths of damaging winds across central Virginia, eventually progressing eastward toward eastern Virginia in the evening.
episodes.215726: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts to Greenbrier County. Surface air temperatures in the mid-70s and dew points in the 60s provided enough instability for storms to intensify. While DCAPE was only a few hundred and low compared to the areas east of the Blue Ridge, surface CAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots allowed severe thunderstorms to evolve and knock over several trees in the area.
episodes.215788: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through eastern Pennsylvania producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
episodes.215789: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through New Jersey producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
episodes.215790: A strong cold front moved into a warm and moist airmass resulting in widespread showers and thunderstorms developing. Some strong to severe thunderstorms moved through the Eastern Shore of Maryland, producing damaging wind gusts and large hail.
episodes.215821: A narrow warm sector along and south of a nearly stationary boundary saw showers and thunderstorms develop in the afternoon hours. Training along the boundary resulted in an isolated flash flooding threat over Ohio.
episodes.215867: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. Thunderstorms ahead of the front developed and delivered damaging wind gusts along and east of the Blue Ridge. Surface air temperatures in the mid-80s and dew points in the 70s provided instability for storms to intensify. SBCAPE of 1000-2000 J/kg and bulk shear of 25-35 knots set favorable conditions for the organization and strengthening of these storms. DCAPE of 900-1200 J/kg resulted in scattered storms delivering damaging wind gusts and numerous downed power lines and trees in north-central North Carolina. A few swaths of damage were reported in the counties of Surry, Stokes, Rockingham, and Caswell with at least one report of a tree falling onto a house.
episodes.215873: A potent mid-level shortwave brought a cold front to the Mid-Atlantic on the afternoon and evening of June 22. episodes.216002: On the night of June 21st, 2026 and into the early morning of June 22nd, 2026, a Mesoscale Convective System moved through southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. This system brought multiple lines of storms and some supercells. Several tornadoes occurred along with flash flooding.
episodes.216100: Many thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall, with amounts anywhere from half an inch up to 1.75 within a few hours. At least minor flooding must have occurred, but no reports of impactful flash flooding. Gusts up to 71 mph were also observed.

events.narrative: Thunderstorm straight line winds in central Martin County near the EF0 tornado, uprooted or snapped several large tree branches and a few whole trees, from Dover Hill to the Shoals area.  Carport damage also occurred.
Water was flowing across IL-33 east of Newton, prompting the closure of the roadway.
US-45 north of Effingham was closed due to high water.
The hail ranged from pea to penny size.
Measured by a Davis Weather Station.
Several power poles were downed.

An EF-0 tornado with 0.49 miles path length, and path width of 85 yards moved through portions of Bartholomew County. The tornado began east of US Highway 31 and continued northeast through a tree line and into a corn field. A convergent wind pattern was noted.  Peak winds were 85 mph.

Thunderstorm rainfall up to 6.00 inches caused widespread flash flooding across central and northern Daviess County, with at least 3 water rescues in Washington and at least 3 additional water rescues in other parts of the county from widespread inundated county roads, some with deep water flowing across;  water additionally flowed into multiple homes.  Flash flooding also impacted west-central Martin County where a CVS in Loogootee had water 2.5 feet deep at its lower back door, while water flowed over several roads north of Loogootee.
A trained spotter reported a brief tornado touchdown west of Edinburg. No|damage was observed.
Measured by a personal weather station.
Maximum hail size increased from dime to half dollar during the event time. The report was relayed by a broadcast media storm chaser. The location is approximate.
Thunderstorm wind gusts, estimated at 80 MPH, destroyed sheds and outbuildings and damaged several roofs. Pivot irrigation systems were also overturned at this location.
Thunderstorm winds downed a power pole with roof damage on Cody Road.
Measured by a personal weather station.
There was a barn damaged near Leipsic off North County Road 600 East.

A NWS ground survey along with public reports determined that an EF0 tornado with a 200 yard wide path initially touched down in a wooded area at the end of County Road H-522 to the southeast of Eminence. The tornado damaged a barn then both broke and uprooted trees as it crossed Highway H and along Highway NN to the Rocky Falls Shut In area off County Road NN-526.
Thunderstorm straight line winds snapped large tree limbs in southeastern Martin County.
A road was closed due to flooding.
A trained spotter reported a brief tornado touchdown near Tower|Hill. No damage was observed.

Thunderstorm rainfall up to 5.00 inches produced flash flooding in central Martin County as far east as the Shoals area.  Water flowed over several roads, including the confluence of Sherfick Stream and Gushing Creek onto Boyd Hollow Road, as well as Beech Creek onto Rama Dye Road where floodwaters where nearly 1,000 feet wide to the north of the creek.
The report was relayed through mPING.

Thunderstorm rainfall of up to 2.50 inches in under 1.5 hours produced flash flooding in the Columbus area, closing County Road 525 East at Base Road, with water also on US Highway 11 just south of County Road 650 South.

The tornado started along County Road 160 doing damage to some trees and a home along the east side of County Road 160. The tornado intensified as it approached Salem Drive, where the worst of the tree damage was noted with roughly 10 trees uprooted in a |small area. The tornado weakened and quickly lifted just to the east of Route 3.
Power lines and trees were down in the area of Harry Hughes Road, Opossum Trot Road, and Williamsburg Drive.

The National Weather Service conducted a storm survey in Meade County, Kentucky for the storms that moved through the region late Sunday night, June 21, 2026.  The nature of the damage was consistent with straight line wind damage between 80 and 85 mph in the Big Bend area of Meade county.||Damage was first observed on Big Bend Road where several trees were uprooted or snapped due to the high winds.  Paradise Bottom Road also had some tree damage.  Damaged areas north of the rock quarry near Big Bend Road had a similar direction facing to the north.  Tree damage continued along Battletown Road north of Battletown.  All damage south of the rock quarry near Big Bend Road was facing to the south. These damage directions would indicate a thunderstorm downburst likely occurred in the Big Bend area with winds spreading out in different divergent directions, evident of a thunderstorm downburst.
There was water over Pleasant Street, Market Street, and County Road 160 in Charlestown.
A tree fell down on Shelbyville Road between Eden Way and Lyndon Lane.
There was a large tree down over the road at the intersection were Rollington Road becomes Fraziertown Road.
There was a large tree blocking Battletown Road near Cedar Flats Road.
The road, 1100 South, was completely underwater between Ferdinand and 50 West.

The National Weather Service conducted a storm survey in Harrison County, Indiana and determined a small EF0 tornado occurred west of Central, IN.  Maximum winds were 85 mph and a max path width of 100 yards.||While most damage in southern Harrison County was consistent with straight line wind damage, a small area west of the town of Central had indications of rotation. A home and farm north of Hisey Road and along Ripperdan Valley Road SW had extensive barn roof damage, as well as damage to a garage.  While the straight line wind damage |was consistently going toward the southeast direction, the damages to the barn and garage were going to the west and southwest toward the center of the tornado passage. Some barn material and barn doors were lofted over the barn, the home, and dropped in the front yard.  There was also impalement of wood planks in the backyard in the northeast direction. Several rotational directions were noted on the property consistent with a small EF0 tornado that formed along the leading edge of the thunderstorm squall line. The tornado continued with sporadic damage into a nearby tree line where there was damage leaning toward the southwest on the north side|of the track, and tree damage leaning toward the northeast on the south side of the track, evident of being pulled into a circulation center along Hisey Road.  Beyond Hisey Road, several trees and barns had damage near and southeast of Central along|Watson Road, Old Goshen Road, and Rehobeth Road. All damages beyond Hisey Road west of Central were in the south to southeast direction, consistent with straight line wind damage.
Multiple trees and power lines were down on Big Bend Road, causing the road to be closed.

This tornado developed just south of Highway 64 and west of Woodland W Road. It moved east-northeast, crossing Woodland W Road and Highway 64, where numerous trees were snapped or uprooted, some fell onto homes, power poles were snapped, and outbuildings were destroyed. The tornado then moved east across two neighborhoods just north of Highway 64. Numerous trees were uprooted or snapped in these neighborhoods and some homes were damaged when trees or large limbs fell onto them. The tornado then turned southeast and crossed Highway 64 near the Highway 23 intersection, where large tree limbs were snapped and signs were damaged. It then crossed the Arkansas River and then Highway 23, and dissipated east of Santa Fe Trail and Aux Arcade Park Road, snapping numerous large tree limbs before it ended. The tornado produced a tornadic debris signature from the KSRX WSR-88D radar. Based on this damage, maximum estimated wind in the tornado was 95 to 105 mph.

A severe thunderstorm produced a strong downburst one mile|northwest of Burke VA with peak winds estimated 90 MPH. While|other minor scattered tree damage was noted outside of the|microburst in the general area, the microburst affected the|communities around Lake Royal. Significant concentrated damage|began along Zion Road between the cross streets of Guinea Drive|and Hillard Lake Road. Tree damage continued along Bridgewood|Drive and Falmead Road before reaching Lake Royal. Through this|area, many, though not all, of the trees were snapped midway,|uprooted, or had large branches snapped off. Trees fell onto cars,|powerlines, roads, and homes with substantial damage. Damage was|unidirectionally pushed to the east northeast in the direction of|storm movement.||As the microburst crossed Lake Royal, the lack of trees and|roughness allowed the winds to accelerate and then blast the|townhomes on the east shore. Several townhomes on that row facing|the lake had significant portions of their roofs lifted off. Winds|were estimated to have peaked at 90 MPH.||On the south side of the lake along Guinea Drive, trees were|snapped onto the road and powerlines. A business park building was|noted to have some damage due to the roof being slightly lifted|temporarily.||Significant tree damage continued to the community on the east|side of Lake Royal with similar tree damage along Lakepoint Drive|west of Guinea Road. Trees and branches were again snapped onto|cars and homes, and townhome fences were pushed down on many|properties. East of Guinea Road, winds lessened and tree damage|became isolated. One further point of note was Burke Road near|Peppercorn Drive where a few trees were downed, one onto a bus|stand and street light.||Throughout the survey, damage was pushed to the northeast in the|direction of storm movement. NWS Doppler Weather Radar KLWX in|Sterling, VA, as well as FAA Terminal Doppler Radars from TDCA|and TADW, displayed thunderstorm downburst signatures at the Burke|location at the time, with no evidence of rotation indicating the|storm being tornadic. Severe straight line thunderstorm downburst|wind gusts can sometimes produce damage equivalent to damage from|EF0 and EF1 tornadoes.||Severe thunderstorms can produce wind gusts equal to EF0 and EF1|tornadoes.||The National Weather Service would like to thanks Fairfax County|Department of Emergency Management and Security for their|assistance.

Several thunderstorms crossed through the region on the evening of June 22, 2026. While there were multiple wind damage reports, the most intense path of damage was near Wye Mills to Cordova with a storm that crossed through near 7 PM. Damage was noted beginning along Old Wye Mills Road where multiple trees had been uprooted. A discontinuous path of damage continued towards the southeast. Along Newtown Road, multiple trees were snapped, with an estimated maximum wind speed of 90 to 100 mph, the highest estimated wind speed along the entire path. Near Saulsbury, a center pivot irrigation system was overturned. Damage path continued with additional damage, primarily tree damage, reported along Blades Road and Asches Acres Road.

A line of severe thunderstorms moved east into southern Maryland on Monday|evening, June 22nd, 2026. This line of storms was the cause of a|widespread severe weather outbreak across portions of both Virginia and|Maryland. One of the thunderstorms developed rotation as it moved out of Saint Mary's|County and across the Patuxent River into Calvert County.||Once that storm moved into Calvert County, terminal doppler|weather radar at Joint Base Andrews (TADW) indicated an|intensifying rotation as it neared Battle Creek, moving quickly|east at 50 mph. A drone video captured the tornado developing, and|tornadic damage was first reported off Honey Cove Court on the|west shore of Battle Creek. Several large branches were snapped on|several trees, and one fell onto a dock. An eyewitness on Shamrock Court|on the east shore of Battle Creek saw the tornado crossing the|creek before they took shelter. More tree damage was reported|along Shamrock Court, as well as along Crane Road and Shannon Way.|An eyewitness off Crane Road passed along a video recording of|rotating and lofted leaf debris. After crossing Shannon Way, the|tornado lifted, although intermittent minor tree damage continued|in Saint Leonard due to downburst winds after the rotation weakened.

A barn near the beginning of the tornado track was destroyed with the debris scattered from NW to|SE of the original structure. Debris from the barn was found over a third of mile to the NE.  ||A double-wide also near the beginning of the path had significant siding damage on the south side and some windows broken out on the west side. The rear end of an SUV parked in gravel next to the double-wide was pushed about 2 feet to the NE while a flag pole in the front yard of the double-wide was blown down in a southwesterly direction. ||From there, the tornado traveled through mostly open fields but did intersect a couple patches of hardwood trees. As it descended a small hill near the middle of the path, several healthy and mature locust trees were uprooted and some trunks were snapped |about 15 feet up and a swirling pattern was noted in the surrounding pasture grass. One tree was observed down near Bud Edge Road and this is assumed to be the end of the tornado track as no further damage was found.
